set.title: ESAT Mathematics 2 — First 10
set.authorship: Original questions. Informed by the 2026 ESAT Mathematics 2 specification, the official Notes on Mathematics, historic ENGAA/NSAA advanced mathematics questions, and TMUA Paper 1 style; no question has been copied.
designIntent: Slightly harder than the Mathematics 1 hook set, while remaining realistic under ESAT time pressure.
Questions reward a short insight or representation change rather than long routine calculation.
The set samples algebra, recurrence relations, coordinate geometry, trigonometry, logarithms, calculus, transformations and binomial expansion.
Every distractor corresponds to a recognisable error and can support targeted feedback.

questions.stemMarkdown:
The line \(y=2x+k\) meets the curve \(y=x^2-4x+7\) at two points.

The \(x\)-coordinates of the two points differ by \(4\).

What is the value of \(k\)?

solution.title: Complete the square before finding the intersections.
stepsMarkdown: Equating the two expressions for \(y\) gives \(x^2-6x+7-k=0\).
So \((x-3)^2=k+2\), and the two roots are \(3\pm\sqrt{k+2}\).

distractorMap.reason: This makes the line tangent to the curve, so the two x-coordinates are equal.
Sets the discriminant equal to 4; the root separation is the square root of the discriminant.
Drops the square root while keeping the factor of 2.
Correct.
Finds \(k+2=4\) but forgets to subtract 2.
Sets \(\sqrt{k+2}=4\), forgetting that 4 is the full gap between the roots.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A sequence is defined by

\[u_1= rac32,\qquad u_{n+1}=2- rac1{u_n}.\]

What is \(u_{20}\)?

solution.title: Generate a few terms, then confirm the pattern.

distractorMap.reason: Uses \(u_n=\dfrac{n}{n+1}\), missing the shift in the pattern.
Uses \(u_n=\dfrac{n+1}{n}\).
Takes the reciprocal of the correct term.
Correct.
Substitutes \(n=21\) instead of \(n=20\).
Assumes the recurrence leaves the starting value unchanged.

questions.stemMarkdown:
Point \(P\) lies on the circle

\[(x-1)^2+(y+2)^2=9,\]

and point \(Q\) lies on the circle

\[(x+5)^2+(y-6)^2=25.\]

What is the greatest possible value of \(PQ\)?

solution.title: Use the line through the two centres.
stepsMarkdown: The centres are \((1,-2)\) and \((-5,6)\), with radii \(3\) and \(5\).
The distance between the centres is \(\sqrt{6^2+8^2}=10\).
The greatest distance occurs at the two outermost points on the line of centres.

distractorMap.reason: Subtracts both radii from the distance between the centres; this gives the minimum gap.
Adds the two radii but ignores the separation of the centres.
Finds only the distance between the centres.
Adds the difference of the radii to the centre distance.
Adds only the larger radius to the centre distance.
Correct.

questions.stemMarkdown:
The equation

\[2\sin^2x=1+\cos x\]

has several solutions in the interval \(0\le x<2\pi\).

What is the sum of all these solutions?

solution.title: Turn the equation into a quadratic in \(\cos x\).

distractorMap.reason: Counts only the solution from \(\cos x=-1\).
Includes \(\pi/3\) and \(\pi\), but misses \(5\pi/3\).
Includes the two solutions from \(\cos x=1/2\), but misses \(x=\pi\).
Includes \(\pi\) and \(5\pi/3\), but misses \(\pi/3\).
Correct.
Treats the upper endpoint \(2\pi\) as an additional solution.

solution.title: Combine the logarithms, then check the domain.

distractorMap.reason: This is an algebraic root, but the logarithms are not defined there.
Makes \(x-1=0\), and \(\log 0\) is undefined.
Makes \(x-3=0\), and \(\log 0\) is undefined.
It is in the domain, but it does not satisfy the equation.
Comes from a one-step arithmetic slip after expanding the product.
Correct.

questions.stemMarkdown:
The function

\[f(x)=x^3-3x^2+k\]

has two stationary points.

For which values of \(k\) do the stationary points lie on opposite sides of the \(x\)-axis?

solution.title: Compare the heights of the two stationary points.
stepsMarkdown: \(f'(x)=3x(x-2)\), so the stationary points occur at \(x=0\) and \(x=2\).
They are on opposite sides of the axis when \(k(k-4)<0\).

distractorMap.reason: When \(k<0\), both stationary points are below the axis.
When \(k>4\), both stationary points are above the axis.
Correct.
This is the range in which the two stationary points are on the same side, or on the axis.
At \(k=0\) or \(k=4\), one stationary point lies on the axis, not on the opposite side.
The vertical shift \(k\) directly controls the two stationary-point heights.

questions.stemMarkdown:
A curve satisfies

\[ rac{dy}{dx}=6x-4\]

and passes through the point \((1,3)\).

What is the minimum value of \(y\)?

solution.title: Recover the curve, then locate its vertex.

distractorMap.reason: This is the x-coordinate of the minimum, not its y-value.
Uses only the \(3x^2\) term at \(x=2/3\).
Uses the correct minimum point but an incorrect integration constant.
Correct.
Assumes the given point is the minimum point.
This is the integration constant, not the minimum value.

The graph of \(y=f(x)\) has a maximum point at \((-2,5)\) and a minimum point at \((4,-1)\).

Define

\[g(x)=3-f(2x-1).\]

What is the maximum point of the graph of \(y=g(x)\)?

solution.title: The minus sign swaps maxima and minima.
stepsMarkdown: The maximum of \(g\) comes from the minimum value of \(f\), which occurs when its input is \(4\).

distractorMap.reason: This is the transformed original maximum, which becomes the new minimum.
Uses the x-position from the original maximum but the height from the new maximum.
Solves the horizontal transformation with the shift in the wrong direction.
Finds the correct x-coordinate but uses the transformed height of the original maximum.
Correct.
Applies \(2x-1\) to the old x-coordinate instead of reversing the transformation.

questions.stemMarkdown: What is the coefficient of \(x^3\) in the expansion of\n\n\[(1+2x)^5(1-x)^2\,?\]

solution.title: Only three pairs of terms can produce \(x^3\).
stepsMarkdown: From \((1+2x)^5\), the coefficients of \(x\), \(x^2\), and \(x^3\) are \(10\), \(40\), and \(80\).

distractorMap.reason: Keeps only the middle contribution \(40(-2)\).
Cancels \(80-80\) but forgets the final contribution of \(10\).
Correct.
Uses only the coefficient of \(x^2\) from the first factor.
Uses only the coefficient of \(x^3\) from \((1+2x)^5\).
Adds the magnitudes of all three contributions and ignores the negative sign.

questions.stemMarkdown:
The function \(f\) is differentiable for every real value of \(x\). Consider the statements:

1. If \(f'(x)>0\) for every real \(x\), then \(f\) is strictly increasing.

2. If \(f'(a)=0\), then \(f\) has a local maximum or a local minimum at \(x=a\).

3. If \(f\) has a local maximum at \(x=a\), then \(f'(a)=0\).

Which statements must be true?

solution.title: A zero derivative is necessary at an interior extremum, but not sufficient.
stepsMarkdown: Statement 1 is true: a positive derivative means the function is strictly increasing.
Statement 2 is false. For example, \(f(x)=x^3\) has \(f'(0)=0\), but no maximum or minimum at \(0\).
Statement 3 is true because \(f\) is differentiable at the local maximum.

distractorMap.reason: Misses the necessary derivative condition at a differentiable local maximum.
Statement 2 is false, while statements 1 and 3 are true.
Misses the fact that a positive derivative gives a strictly increasing function.
Treats every stationary point as a turning point and misses statement 3.
Correct.
Incorrectly assumes that \(f'(a)=0\) is enough to guarantee an extremum.
